lessons.title: How Do I Feel?
objectives: Name six basic feelings
Recognise feelings from faces
explanation: Feelings are what happens inside us when things happen around us. Some feelings are happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised and calm.
Our faces show our feelings. A smile can show happy. Tears can show sad. A frown and tight fists can show angry. Wide eyes can show surprised or scared.
All feelings are okay to have. Everyone feels sad or angry sometimes. What matters is what we do with our feelings — and that we can talk about them.

vocabulary.meaning: what happens inside us, like happy or sad

examples: 😀 Getting a hug from Grandma — happy.
😢 Dropping your ice cream — sad.

story.text: In the morning, Momo got a new kite — happy! At lunch, it got stuck in a tree — sad. Kiko laughed — Momo felt angry! Then a loud thunderclap — scared! Mama Bear gave a big hug, and Momo felt calm. "So many feelings in one day," Momo sighed, "and they all came and went."

lessons.title: Body Clues
objectives: Notice where feelings show in the body
Use body clues to name a feeling
explanation: Feelings show up in our bodies! When we are angry, our face may feel hot and our fists tight. When we are nervous, we might feel "butterflies" in our tummy.
When we are sad, our body might feel heavy and slow. When we are happy, we might feel light and bouncy, like we want to jump.
Noticing these body clues helps us know what we are feeling — and then we can do something to help ourselves.

lessons.title: I Feel… Because…
objectives: Say what caused a feeling using "I feel… because…"

explanation: Feelings have causes. "I feel happy because my friend shared her crayons." "I feel cross because my tower fell down."
The same thing can make different people feel different ways. Thunder might make one child scared and another excited!
Feelings don't last forever. They come and go like weather — a cloudy feeling can turn sunny again.

lessons.title: My Calm-Down Toolbox
objectives: Use at least three calming strategies
Choose a strategy that works for them
prerequisites: Recognises big feelings in the body
explanation: Sometimes feelings get very big — like a volcano about to erupt! It's okay to feel angry or upset, but we try not to hurt ourselves, others or things.
Calming tools help: take slow belly breaths (smell the flower, blow out the candle), count slowly to ten, squeeze a soft toy, go to a quiet calm corner, or ask for a hug.
Different tools work for different people. When the feeling is smaller, we can talk about what happened.

vocabulary.meaning: help a big feeling get smaller

examples: "Smell the flower" (breathe in), "blow out the candle" (breathe out).

lessons.title: Empathy Steps
objectives: Notice and name how someone else might feel
Respond kindly to someone's feelings
explanation: Empathy means trying to understand how someone else feels — imagining being in their shoes.
Empathy steps: Notice (look at their face and body), Wonder (how might they feel, and why?), and Respond (say or do something kind: "Are you okay? Do you want to play with me?").
Empathy doesn't mean you must feel exactly the same, or fix everything. Sometimes just listening helps a lot.
examples: Seeing a classmate alone at lunch and inviting them to sit with you.
Saying "That must have been scary" when a friend tells you about a dog chasing them.

lessons.title: Just the Right Feeling Word
objectives: Use precise feeling words
Explain differences between similar feelings
explanation: There are many more feeling words than happy, sad and angry. Happy can be proud, excited, grateful or content. Sad can be disappointed, lonely or hurt.
Angry can be frustrated (when something is hard), annoyed (a little angry), or jealous (wanting what someone else has). Scared can be worried, nervous or terrified.
Using the exact word helps others understand you — and helps you understand yourself. "I'm frustrated because this puzzle is hard" is clearer than "I'm mad!"

vocabulary.meaning: sad because something didn't happen as hoped

lessons.title: Two Feelings at Once
objectives: Identify mixed feelings in situations
Distinguish feelings, thoughts and actions
explanation: We can feel two or more feelings at the same time. Moving to a new city might feel exciting and sad. Performing on stage might feel nervous and thrilled.
Feelings, thoughts and actions are connected but different. Feeling: "I'm nervous." Thought: "What if I forget my lines?" Action: practising, or avoiding the stage.
We can't always choose our feelings, but we can notice our thoughts and choose our actions.

vocabulary.meaning: more than one feeling at the same time

lessons.title: Bouncing Back
objectives: Use growth mindset language
Use problem-solving steps after a setback
explanation: Resilience is the ability to bounce back after difficult times, like a ball that bounces after it drops. Everyone faces setbacks: losing a match, a bad mark, a fight with a friend.
Growth mindset language helps: instead of "I can't do this", say "I can't do this YET." Mistakes help our brains learn.
Problem-solving steps: calm down, name the problem, think of options, choose one and try it, then check how it went. And it's always okay to ask for help.

lessons.title: The Five Parts of Emotional Intelligence
objectives: Describe the components of emotional intelligence
Reflect on personal strengths and areas to grow
prerequisites: Recognises mixed feelings and uses coping strategies
explanation: Emotional intelligence (EQ) means recognising, understanding and managing emotions — your own and others'. A popular model, from psychologist Daniel Goleman, describes five parts.
Self-awareness (knowing your emotions), self-regulation (managing them), motivation (using emotions to pursue goals), empathy (understanding others) and social skills (handling relationships well).
Emotions influence decisions — sometimes helpfully (fear keeps us safe), sometimes unhelpfully (anger leads to words we regret). Pausing before reacting is a key EQ skill.

context.text: Emotional intelligence is a widely used framework; psychologists debate how best to define and measure it, and different models exist.

vocabulary.meaning: the ability to understand and manage emotions

examples: Pausing and breathing before replying to an annoying message.
Noticing a friend is upset even when they say "I'm fine".

lessons.title: Understanding Stress
objectives: Distinguish everyday stress from anxiety that needs help
Use healthy coping strategies
explanation: Stress is the body's response to challenges. A little stress can help — it focuses us before an exam or match. Too much stress for too long can affect sleep, mood, appetite and health.

Anxiety is a feeling of worry or fear. Everyone feels anxious sometimes, but if worry is very strong, lasts a long time, or stops someone from doing everyday things, it's important to talk to a trusted adult or professional.

Healthy coping: breathing exercises, exercise, sleep, talking to someone, breaking tasks into small steps, limiting news and social media, and doing things you enjoy. Unhealthy coping — like avoiding everything or hurting yourself — makes things worse; get help.

vocabulary.meaning: the body's response to challenges or pressure
a way of handling difficult feelings
a trained person such as a counsellor or doctor

examples: Feeling nervous before exams and then fine afterwards — usual stress.
Worrying so much you can't sleep for weeks — time to get help.

story.title: Exam Week
story.text: Before her exams, Riya couldn't sleep and felt her chest tighten. She told her mother, who helped her make a study timetable with breaks, and they went for evening walks. When the worry stayed strong, they talked to the school counsellor, who taught her breathing techniques. Slowly, she felt in control again.

lessons.title: Emotions and the Brain
objectives: Describe brain regions involved in emotion
Compare theories and cultural frameworks of emotion
explanation: Brain areas work together in emotion. The amygdala helps detect threats quickly; the prefrontal cortex helps plan, reason and regulate emotional responses. In adolescence, the prefrontal cortex is still developing.

Scientists have proposed different theories: some emphasise bodily reactions leading to feelings; others emphasise how we interpret situations; many modern researchers see emotions as constructed from body signals, context and concepts learned in culture.

Indian aesthetics offers the rasa theory from the Natyashastra: art evokes emotional "flavours" such as shringara (love), karuna (compassion), raudra (anger), bhayanaka (fear) and shanta (peace, added by later theorists).

context.text: Theories of emotion are actively debated; no single theory is universally accepted.
The Natyashastra lists eight rasas; later scholars such as Abhinavagupta discussed shanta as a ninth.

vocabulary.meaning: a brain region involved in detecting threats and emotional responses
the brain region for planning and self-control
in Indian aesthetics, the emotional essence evoked by art

examples: Jumping at a sudden noise before you know what it is.

lessons.title: The Mental Health Continuum
objectives: Explain mental health as a continuum
Plan how to support a friend and reduce stigma
explanation: Mental health is a continuum, from thriving to struggling, and people move along it over time. Everyone has mental health, just like physical health.

Stigma — negative attitudes about mental illness — stops many people from seeking help. Language matters: saying "a person with depression" rather than insulting labels, and treating mental illness like any other health condition.

To support a friend: notice changes, ask "How are you really?", listen without judging, encourage professional help, and tell a trusted adult if they may be in danger. Look after your own wellbeing too.

vocabulary.meaning: a mental health condition with persistent low mood

examples: A friend who stops enjoying activities and withdraws may need support.

story.title: The Friend Who Went Quiet
story.text: Kavya noticed her friend Dev had gone quiet, stopped playing cricket and skipped lunch. She asked, "How are you really?" He shrugged at first, then admitted he felt low all the time. Kavya listened, then said, "Can we talk to Mr. Rao together?" The counsellor helped Dev find support. Months later, Dev thanked her.
